readings.title: Street gardens and storm water
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On a busy street in Brookdale, a row of shallow gardens now separates the sidewalk from traffic. They look decorative, but they were built to solve a practical problem. During heavy rain, water once rushed across the road and entered nearby shops. The gardens collect part of that water before it reaches the drains. Soil and plant roots slow the flow, while openings in the curb guide water into each garden.

The city began with six gardens as a one-year experiment. Engineers measured water levels after storms, and local college students recorded the insects and birds they saw. The results were modest but useful. Streets beside the gardens flooded less often, and the planted areas attracted more pollinators than ordinary grass strips did. Shop owners also reported that the street had become a more pleasant place to walk.

The project was not trouble-free. In the first summer, several gardens filled with litter, and two types of plants failed in the heat. The city replaced those plants with species better suited to dry weather and added signs explaining that the gardens were part of the drainage system. A business group organized monthly cleanups. Maintenance costs then fell because city workers no longer had to remove rubbish as often.

Brookdale plans to build more rain gardens, but officials do not consider them a complete answer to flooding. Large storms can still overwhelm underground pipes. The gardens are one part of a wider plan that includes repairing old drains, creating more open ground, and warning residents about severe weather. The experiment shows that small changes at street level can support larger systems, especially when residents understand their purpose and help care for them.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

options.D: Old drains should all be abandoned.

readings.title: Protecting time for difficult work
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Many office workers begin the day by opening email and chat applications. These tools make it easy to ask a quick question, but constant messages can divide attention. At a small engineering company, employees complained that they had little uninterrupted time for difficult tasks. The company responded by testing two daily quiet hours, from 9:30 to 11:30, when internal messages were discouraged unless a matter was urgent.

Managers did not simply switch off the software. Before the trial, each team agreed on what counted as urgent and chose a phone number for emergencies. Employees could still contact customers, and colleagues working in different time zones could arrange exceptions. This preparation mattered. In an earlier attempt, a manager had announced a no-message morning without discussing exceptions. Some employees worried that they would be blamed for replying late, so they kept checking their inboxes.

After six weeks, the company compared the trial period with the previous six weeks. The number of internal messages changed very little because most conversations happened later in the day. However, employees reported fewer unwanted interruptions in the morning, and teams completed design reviews slightly faster. Customer response times did not worsen. Several employees still disliked the policy, especially those whose jobs depended on frequent coordination. The company therefore allowed these teams to choose shorter quiet periods.

The trial did not prove that one schedule would suit every workplace. Its more useful lesson was that a communication rule should match the work being done. Tasks requiring concentration benefit from protected time, while tasks requiring rapid cooperation need easier contact. A rule also works better when employees help define it and know how genuine emergencies will be handled.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

options.B: A lack of uninterrupted working time.

readings.title: Learning at a repair cafe
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On the first Saturday of every month, volunteers in Westford turn a school hall into a repair cafe. Residents bring broken lamps, clothes, bicycles, and small appliances. Instead of leaving an item at a counter, each visitor sits beside a volunteer and takes part in the repair. The service is free, although visitors may pay for replacement parts or make a small donation. There is no promise that every object will work again.

The cafe began when its founder, Elena Ruiz, noticed how many usable objects were being thrown away. She first saw the project as a way to reduce waste. Soon she discovered another benefit. People who felt nervous about tools became more confident after watching a volunteer test a wire or adjust a bicycle brake. Some returned later as volunteers themselves. Retired technicians also found a place to share skills that were no longer part of their daily work.

Not every object can be saved. Modern products may be sealed with glue, and spare parts can cost more than a replacement. For safety reasons, volunteers refuse to repair certain gas-powered devices. When a repair is impossible, they explain why and suggest responsible recycling. Ruiz says an honest failure is valuable if the visitor learns how a product was made and what to consider when buying another one.

Last year, volunteers examined 640 objects and returned 410 to working use. These figures do not show the full environmental effect: a repaired toaster and a repaired coat save different amounts of material. Nor do the numbers measure conversations and skills shared in the hall. The cafe therefore reports both repair totals and visitors' stories. Together, they explain the project's practical results and its less visible contribution to community learning.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: What makes notes useful
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Students often ask whether taking notes by hand is better than typing them. Handwriting is usually slower, so a student cannot record every spoken word. This limitation can encourage the writer to select main ideas and express them more briefly. Typing allows a fuller record, but it also makes copying without thought easier. Neither observation means that one tool is always superior to the other.

In a study workshop, tutor Mei gives two groups the same short lecture. One group uses paper and the other uses laptops. She asks both groups to identify the speaker's claim, supporting examples, and unanswered questions. The resulting notes vary greatly within each group. Some handwritten pages are disorganized lists, while some typed pages show clear relationships. Mei uses these examples to explain that the tool alone does not determine how deeply someone processes information.

The next stage happens after the lecture. Students review their notes within a day, while the discussion is still reasonably fresh. They fill gaps, check unfamiliar words, and turn headings into questions. Rather than repeatedly reading the page, they close it and write a short summary from memory. This effort shows them which ideas they can explain and which ones they need to study again. It may feel harder than looking at highlighted sentences, but it produces more useful feedback.

Mei does not require everyone to adopt the same system. A student with a hand injury may need a keyboard, and a technical lecture may demand diagrams. She asks students to choose a method that suits the situation and supports active thinking. Good notes are not simply a beautiful record of what a teacher said. They are working materials that help a learner organize, question, and later recover important ideas.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

translation.stem: Public libraries are changing as the needs of their communities change. In addition to lending books, many libraries now offer study rooms, computer access, language classes, and practical workshops. These services are especially important for people who cannot easily find quiet space or reliable technology elsewhere. A library, however, cannot provide every possible service. Its staff must talk with local residents, examine how existing resources are used, and set clear priorities. Partnerships with schools, volunteer groups, and businesses can also extend what a library is able to do. When new programs are planned carefully, the library remains more than a place for storing books. It becomes a shared public space where people can learn, solve problems, and take part in community life.
translation.referenceAnswer: 公共图书馆随着社区需求的变化而改变。除了借书，许多图书馆如今还提供自习室、电脑、语言课程和实用讲座。这些服务对难以在其他地方找到安静空间或可靠技术设备的人尤其重要。然而图书馆不可能提供所有服务。工作人员必须与当地居民交流，了解现有资源的使用情况并明确重点。与学校、志愿者团体和企业合作也能扩大服务能力。新项目经过认真规划，图书馆就不仅是藏书场所，而成为人们学习、解决问题和参与社区生活的共享公共空间。
translation.explanation: 注意 in addition to（除……之外）、set priorities（确定重点）以及 where 引导的定语从句。

writing.stem: Write an essay entitled Being Present in Conversation. Describe phone checking during face-to-face conversations, explain its effects, and suggest practical improvements. Write at least 100 English words.
writing.sampleAnswer:
It is common to see people checking messages while someone is speaking to them. A quick look at a phone may seem harmless, but repeated interruptions can make the other person feel ignored. They also cause the phone user to miss details, so a conversation may take longer or lead to misunderstandings.

We can improve the situation with a few simple habits. Before an important conversation, we can silence the phone and keep it in a bag. If we are waiting for an urgent message, we should explain this at the beginning and check only when necessary. Giving someone our full attention shows respect and helps us respond thoughtfully. Technology is useful, but the person in front of us deserves our attention during a conversation.
writing.explanation: 可按现象、影响、建议展开；举例说明被忽视和信息遗漏，再提出静音与事先解释等措施。
